The goal of this notebook is to iteratively define the layers of a reproducible
environment, define the contract between those layers, then test that contract.

In my experience, building the reproducible scientific
software stack is something of a journey. It's rarely
a single step, and to assume as much is to actually set
oneself up for disappointment. It can take a while to
iterate several times to get the right combination of
tools, libraries, and packages that work together in a
reproducible way. Worse still, it can be incredibly
frustrating, and as one's patience wears thin, one can be tempted to 
take shortcuts that you don't write down, which means when
you clone the environment or project to a new system,
or even just to rerun it a few months later,
you find yourself in the dreaded dependency hell.

To remedy this, we came up with this recipe-style
workbench tool. We hope that by stepping through the
notebooks in order, users will be better able to
not only reproducibly build their environments, 
but also understand the layers and composition of the environment
intuitively, so that debugging and troubleshooting
is easier.

Here's a summary of the layers and their owners:

- [Singularity](https://singularity.hpcng.org/) provides the isolated 
Linux runtime and binds the project directory and its working files at 
`/work`.
- The platform image provides general essential tools: Spack, `rv`, 
`uv`, `arf`, `code`, and the `/work` directory. If necessary,
the platform image can also install a limited set of system
dependencies.
- [Spack](https://spack.readthedocs.io/) largely owns 
the resolution of the scientific system dependencies such as R
and Python, and package dependencies like `libuv`, `zlib`, etc., 
as well as compilers, headers, and shared libraries.
- The Spack `view` exposes the system layer at one stable 
prefix: `/work/.spack-env/view`.
- The activation script makes the Spack view discoverable to 
compilers, linkers, package builds, and runtime processes.
- `rv` owns the project's R package dependencies.
- `uv` owns the project's Python package dependencies.
- The project source tree (bound at `/work`) owns analysis 
code, project configuration, lockfiles, and runtime state.

Durable writable Singularity sandboxes on shared `/n` 
filesystems are unreliable, so instead, we use disposable 
node-local sandboxes for exploration and layering, then 
build final unwritable SIFs for durable runtime. In other words,
we tinker in a sandbox throughout this series notebooks,
reproducibly adding layers to our final concrete
environment. When we are ready, we bake the final recipe
into a solid SIF container; at runtime, we bind the project
directory into the container, activate the environment within,
and work away! So long as all changes to files happen within
the `/work` directory, and all scripted, runtime level 
installations are done through Spack, `rv`, or `uv`, we have a 
shippable containerized environment that can be 
reproduced on any system with Singularity.

To get started, copy the contents of the `notebooks/rse_workbench` 
folder into a new `notebooks/projects/<project-name>` directory, 
and run the notebooks in order. The notebooks are designed to 
be read and executed in order, but you can also skip around 
if you are already familiar with the concepts.

There are a number of helper functions defined in the `rse_workbench` 
package that are used throughout the notebooks. For your project,
just make sure you import the functions you need. Re-rendering the
RSE Workbench will re-export the module functions to `src`, so
if you need to make adjustments to the functions or add new ones, you 
can do that in the `rse_workbench` folder's notebooks and re-render
the project.

Before treating the environment as ready, ensure you have a record of:

- Which branch owns this project.
- Which SIF was built.
- Which Spack specs were added beyond the defaults.
- Which R and Python packages were added beyond the defaults.
- Whether `/work/env/check-system-deps.sh` passes inside the SIF.
- Whether `rv sync` completed without ignored failures.
- The VSCode tunnel job ID and log path.

---

In closing, when building environments, keep in mind the following 
principles; you may come up with your own or modify these,
but the point is to define your problem clearly, know the constraints
of both your scenario and your ability to problem-solve,
and be flexible, but methodical, as you test your assumptions:

- Do not make one tool responsible for the whole scientific software stack.
- Define layers, define the contract between layers, then test that contract.
- The project is bound into the container at `/work`.
- Spack owns the system dependency layer.
- `rv` owns the R package layer.
- `uv` owns the Python package layer.
- A Spack view makes the system layer available at one stable prefix.
- Installing a library is not the same as making it discoverable.
- Avoid project-level Spack recipes unless there is a strong reason to use them.
